surfaces.part: front wall with arched opening and bars, plus lower stone bands

answer.evidence: The width profile grows from 4 px at row 1 to 40 px at rows 9-13. That forms a sloped roof plane across rows 1-11, with a lighter left slope and a darker right slope. A dark eave line at row 12 ends the roof, and below it the roof overhangs a 30-row front face (rows 13-42). The front face holds the dark arched opening with bars and horizontal stone courses. The roof reads as a real top surface, not just a rim, so this is a three-quarter view. No receding side face is drawn.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small stone crypt arch with moss and vines. It has about 4 stone steps (pale highlight, light grey, mid grey, dark grey) and a dark doorway interior. Measured visible tones per tile are 21 against 12 and 10 for the references, and near-flat coverage is 4% against 0%, so the numbers do not flag it as shallow. The outline is the problem: 89% of dark edge pixels are near-neutral, against 7-9% for the references, so it reads as a neutral black/grey line. The references use tinted dark tones (dark brown, red-brown) and separate forms by value. The candidate's stone is shaded in only a few grey steps, against the 5-6 steps per material on the references. The stone blocks show some brick texture and the moss gives variation, but the piece is small and visibly thinner than the references' roof and wall detail. The tone count is probably inflated by the moss and vine accents. The neutral outline gives it the sticker look the standard rejects, so it fails.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small stone crypt entrance with a pale stone arch, a dark interior, and vines. The measured facts are mixed. Visible tones per tile are 21 against 10-12 for the references, and near-flat coverage is 4%, so the numbers do not say it is thin. But 89% of its dark edge pixels are near-neutral, against 7-9% for the references. That matches the picture, where the dark opening and the lines between stones are neutral black or grey with no brown or purple lean, which is the sticker-style outline the standard rejects. Shading is shallower than the references: the stone has about 4 steps (light, mid, dark, black) and no per-stone shading like the h112 stone wall, with its stones shaded one by one. Texture is present (brick-like courses, moss, vine pixels) but sparse and mostly confined to the arch. At this scale the piece looks flatter and more cut-out than the references, which carry tinted dark tones and richer tile and plaster grain. Neutral-black outlines and shallower ramps mean it falls short of the Beodeul bar.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small stone crypt portal about 1.5 tiles wide, with ivy, a dark opening and a stone-brick base. Measured facts favour it: 21 visible tones per tile against 10-12 for the references, 4% near-flat coverage, and no large flat fills. The outline is the problem. 89% of its dark edge pixels are near-neutral, against 7-9% for the references, so the interior of the doorway and the edges read as neutral black and grey lines. This is the sticker look, not the dark material tone outline Beodeul uses. The stone blocks carry only about 4 lightness steps, with a pale top lintel, mid-grey blocks and a near-black opening, and they are shaded less stone by stone than the reference's cobble wall. The piece also has no roof, so it is much simpler than the full houses. Despite the good tone counts, the neutral outline and shallower ramps make it fall short of the Beodeul standard.
